Family Health

Does a burning nose mean COVID? Symptoms, testing and other causes

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Nasal burning can happen during a respiratory illness, but it cannot identify COVID on its own. Other symptoms, exposure, testing and the severity of illness are more useful guides.

A burning nose is a symptom, not a COVID test

COVID-19 is caused by SARS-CoV-2, the coronavirus identified in 2019. It can affect the upper airway, including the nose, and people have described irritation or burning during infection. However, burning is not a distinctive sign that confirms COVID, and there is no dependable frequency estimate that makes it useful as a stand-alone test.

A blocked or runny nose is recognised among possible symptoms. The same sensations may occur with a cold, allergy, dryness or exposure to an irritant. Consider the wider picture: a recent exposure, other symptoms, whether people around you are ill and your risk of complications. If an infection is possible, testing and sensible precautions are more informative than comparing how the burning feels.

Inflammation and irritation have several possible causes

The nasal lining can become irritated by dry air, smoke, strong fragrances, allergy or a respiratory infection. Swelling and mucus can make breathing through the nose uncomfortable. Postnasal drainage may irritate the throat as well. A symptom that started after using a spray or encountering a strong smell may have a different explanation from one that appears with fever and a new cough.

Sinusitis means inflammation of the spaces around the nose and face. It often follows a viral illness, while some cases involve bacteria; invasive fungal infection is a much less common and distinct problem. Nasal blockage does not automatically progress to bacterial or fungal disease, and burning alone does not establish any of these diagnoses. Persistent or worsening facial pain, fever or symptoms after initial improvement deserve medical advice.

What the early nasal-symptom research actually showed

A 2020 publication brought together reports covering 1,773 laboratory-confirmed cases. It recorded nasal congestion in 4.1% and a runny nose in 2.1%. These were early reported proportions from studies with different methods and incomplete recording of some symptoms. They should not be treated as current rates for everyone with COVID or as evidence that a runny nose makes infection unlikely.

Other early reports described smell or taste changes in substantial numbers of patients, but estimates depended heavily on who was studied and how symptoms were collected. One pilot study examined the first 237 clinician submissions to an anosmia reporting tool: 73% noticed smell loss before their COVID diagnosis, and 26.6% described it as the initial symptom. Because these were selected smell-related reports, neither figure describes all infected people.

Unusual sinus complications need careful interpretation

A March 2021 case report described a 52-year-old man with COVID and diabetes who developed severe right-sided sinus disease, swelling around the eye and damage involving the hard palate. Surgery identified a thrombosed artery, and bacterial and fungal cultures were negative. The authors discussed a possible connection to COVID-related clotting and inflammation, but one case cannot establish that the virus was the sole cause.

A separate report published online in February 2021 described three cases of invasive fungal sinusitis associated with COVID. Such infections can be life-threatening, particularly in people with impaired immunity or severe illness. These unusual reports do not show that ordinary nasal burning predicts a dangerous sinus complication. Severe facial swelling, eye pain or swelling, visual changes or rapidly worsening illness warrants urgent assessment rather than home treatment.

Why researchers study cells inside the nose

The nasal lining is an important site of contact between respiratory viruses and the body. Research has examined ACE2, a protein that SARS-CoV-2 can use as a receptor, and entry-related enzymes such as TMPRSS2. Early single-cell studies found relevant gene expression in nasal secretory and ciliated epithelial cells. Ciliated cells help move mucus, while secretory cells contribute to the protective lining.

ACE2 is also present outside the nose, including in other respiratory and digestive tissues. Cell and animal experiments can help researchers understand entry and replication, but they do not show that a burning sensation measures receptor activity. Entry pathways also vary with the experimental setting and viral variant. Do not try to alter these proteins with an unproven nasal product or stop a prescribed medicine because of a laboratory finding.

Look beyond the nose without relying on a symptom checklist

Possible COVID symptoms include fever or chills, cough, sore throat, fatigue, headache, body aches, congestion, a runny nose, new smell or taste changes, nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Breathing difficulty can occur. Some reports also describe red eyes or skin changes, but these findings have many other causes. A person may have only a few symptoms, and lack of fever or smell loss does not exclude infection.

The pattern has changed across variants and with prior immunity. Older adults, people with certain medical conditions or weakened immune systems, and pregnant people may need particular attention to early assessment and treatment. Do not assume that a mild start guarantees the illness will remain mild. Tell the clinician when symptoms began, because that date can determine which treatments are still useful.

COVID, flu, colds and allergies overlap

COVID and influenza can both cause fever, aches, marked fatigue, headache, cough and a sore throat. Colds commonly involve sneezing, congestion and a runny nose; loss of smell can also occur when the nose is blocked. Symptoms alone cannot reliably distinguish these infections. Sneezing does not rule out COVID, and flu can cause serious breathing problems too.

Allergies often bring an itchy nose or throat, repeated sneezing, watery or red eyes and symptoms linked to a trigger or season. They can also cause a cough, and may aggravate asthma or wheezing. Fever is not typical of an uncomplicated allergy. A familiar allergy pattern is a clue, but an allergy and an infection can occur together. New breathlessness should not be dismissed as “just allergies” without following your asthma plan or obtaining appropriate help.

Testing and early treatment guide the next step

If COVID is possible, use a test according to its instructions and local availability. One negative rapid antigen result does not exclude infection, especially early on. Current US guidance recommends that symptomatic people obtain at least two negative antigen tests 48 hours apart, or discuss a suitable laboratory test. Follow the product and local guidance; seek care sooner if you feel very unwell.

People at higher risk should contact a clinician promptly even with mild symptoms. Antiviral treatments generally need to begin within the first five to seven days, depending on the medicine, and require an interaction and suitability check. Do not wait for severe illness or for every repeat test before asking about treatment. Rest, ordinary fluids and an appropriate fever or pain medicine may help comfort, but do not replace assessment when symptoms worsen.

Protect others using current local guidance

Stay home and reduce close contact when you have respiratory symptoms that are not better explained by another cause. Improve ventilation, use a well-fitting mask when appropriate and take particular care around people at higher risk. Follow your local public-health advice and any rules for your workplace, school or healthcare setting rather than applying an old universal ten-day isolation rule.

As an example, current US community guidance allows a return to normal activities once symptoms have been improving overall and there has been no fever without fever-reducing medicine for at least 24 hours. Extra precautions are advised for the following five days. If fever returns or you worsen, stay home again. This does not mean everyone is non-infectious at a fixed time, and healthcare or immunocompromised-person advice may differ.

Know when home care is no longer enough

Seek emergency help for significant trouble breathing, persistent chest pain or pressure, new confusion, inability to wake or stay awake, or a concerning pale, grey or blue colour of the lips or skin. Colour changes can be harder to recognise on darker skin; do not wait for a visible change if breathing or alertness is abnormal. Tell emergency staff that a respiratory infection may be involved.

Arrange medical advice for worsening or persistent nasal symptoms, significant facial pain, ongoing fever or a reduced ability to drink. Severe swelling around an eye or a change in vision needs urgent care. For mild irritation, avoiding smoke and fragrances and using an appropriate plain saline nasal product may help. Do not put disinfectants into the nose or use antibiotics, antifungals or concentrated oils without a proper assessment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

COVID, flu, colds and allergies have overlapping symptoms.

Early selected studies and rare case reports do not establish today’s symptom frequency.

Testing, timely treatment for higher-risk people and current local precautions are more useful than an isolated nasal sensation.

How BeMama can help

Record symptom onset and check current local testing advice. If someone is at higher risk, ask about treatment early instead of waiting for a classic symptom pattern.

When to seek help

Breathing difficulty, persistent chest pain, new confusion or inability to stay awake requires emergency help. Severe eye swelling or visual changes also needs urgent assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Burning alone cannot confirm or exclude COVID.
  • Sneezing and a runny nose do not rule it out.
  • One negative antigen test may need repeating.
  • Use current local advice rather than an old isolation timetable.

Frequently asked questions

Is burning inside the nose a reliable COVID symptom?

No. It has several possible causes and cannot diagnose COVID by itself.

Does nasal blockage mean a fungal infection is developing?

No. Most nasal symptoms do not indicate invasive fungal disease. Severe facial or eye symptoms need assessment.

Do the early 4.1% and 2.1% figures apply now?

No. They came from early reports with differing symptom recording and are not current population estimates.

Did 73% of all people with COVID lose smell before diagnosis?

No. That finding came from 237 selected clinician reports to a smell-loss tool, not a representative sample of all infections.

Can sneezing rule out COVID?

No. Symptoms overlap and change. Testing and context are more useful than that rule.

Can allergies cause a cough?

Yes. Allergic rhinitis can cause coughing and may aggravate asthma. New or significant breathing difficulty still needs attention.

Is one negative rapid test enough?

Not always. Symptomatic people may need repeat antigen testing 48 hours later or a laboratory test according to local guidance.

Should a high-risk person wait until symptoms are severe?

No. Ask about treatment promptly, because antiviral options have short start windows and need a suitability review.

Must everyone isolate for exactly ten days?

No. Follow current local guidance. Requirements differ by setting and may change over time.

Can laboratory findings about ACE2 suggest a home nasal treatment?

No. Entry-factor research does not validate a home remedy or justify stopping prescribed medicines.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
